body.heading: The problem
paragraphs: A farmer arrives at a river with a wolf, a goat and a cabbage. The boat carries the farmer plus just one of the three. If left alone together, the wolf will eat the goat, and the goat will eat the cabbage. How does everyone cross safely?

This puzzle is over a thousand years old — it appears in a collection of puzzles attributed to Alcuin of York, a scholar at the court of Charlemagne, written around the year 800. Generations of children have worried over that goat.

body.heading: The way across
paragraphs: The key realisation: the goat is the troublemaker in both pairings, so the goat must never be left with either companion — and sometimes something must be brought back. Take the goat across first. Return alone. Take the wolf across — and bring the goat back.

Now take the cabbage across, leaving the goat safely behind. Return alone one last time, collect the goat, and cross. Seven crossings, no lunches. The backward trip with the goat feels wrong, and that is exactly why the puzzle survives: the solution requires undoing progress.

body.heading: Try it: act it out and extend it
paragraphs: Act the puzzle out with toys or labelled cups on a table — moving the pieces makes the dangerous pairs visible, and younger solvers can spot trouble before it happens.

Then try the harder cousins. Missionaries and cannibals (three of each, a boat for two, and one group must never outnumber the other on either bank) is the famous grown-up version. The same patient, one-crossing-at-a-time thinking will carry you through.

takeaway: The river crossing teaches a deep puzzle lesson: sometimes the only way forward is to carry something back.
